title: When should P/B be used?
subtitle: Most useful for asset-heavy or financial businesses
openingQuestion: The P/B (Price-to-Book) ratio is most commonly used to value which type of company?
openingOptions: Banks, insurers, real estate - where book value reflects real asset value fairly closely (cash, loans, property)
A tech company with large intangible assets (brand, patents)
A newly founded company that has no assets yet
explanation: P/B = Share price / book value per share. Most useful for industries where the assets on the balance sheet reflect real economic value fairly accurately: banks (cash, loans), insurance, real estate. For a tech company with many intangible assets not fully recognized on the books (brand, user data), P/B is far less meaningful.

diagram.label: Divide share price by book value per share
Ask: does the book value reflect real economic value?
Banks, insurance, real estate: fairly close, usable
Tech companies: intangible assets aren't on the books, the ratio loses meaning

realWorldExample.description: Bank analysts usually prioritize P/B over P/E, because a bank's assets (mainly loans and deposits) are reflected fairly closely on the balance sheet compared to their real economic value.

quiz.question: Is a P/B below 1 (share price lower than book value) always a sign the stock is 'cheap' and worth buying?
options: No - a low P/B can be due to poor-quality assets or a low ROE
Yes, you should always buy right away once P/B drops below 1x book value
P/B below 1 only happens to a company about to go bankrupt, so it must be avoided
P/B never actually drops below 1 in real markets
quiz.explanation: A low P/B can be a genuine value opportunity, but it can also be a 'value trap' - the market has correctly priced it in because of legitimate concerns: poor asset quality, hidden bad debt at a bank.

quiz.question: A tech company has P/B = 15x (very high compared to a bank's typical 1-2x). Does that mean tech stocks are being unreasonably overvalued?
options: Correct, a high P/B always means unreasonably overvalued
No - the value lies in intangible assets not yet recorded on the books
Banks always have higher P/B than tech companies in the market
P/B only applies to banks, not usable for tech at all
quiz.explanation: This is exactly why P/B isn't suitable for valuing tech companies - their real value lies in intangible assets that don't appear on the balance sheet.

quiz.question: Share price 30,000 dong, book value per share 25,000 dong. What is P/B?
options: 5,000 dong (= 30,000 − 25,000, taking the difference)
0.83x (= 25,000 ÷ 30,000, dividing the wrong way round)
1.5x (= 30,000 ÷ 20,000, wrong book value)
quiz.explanation: P/B = Price / Book Value per Share = 30,000/25,000 = 1.2. The market is paying 1.2 dong for every dong of net assets on the books - a modest level, commonly seen at banks.

quiz.question: Why is a bank's P/B more meaningful than a software company's P/B?
options: Because banks are required to revalue assets every quarter
Because banks have a much larger asset scale than software companies
Because software companies aren't allowed to record equity
Because a bank's assets are loans, recorded fairly close to real value
quiz.explanation: Book value is only useful when it reflects what actually creates value. For a bank that's its loan portfolio sitting right on the balance sheet; for software it's the brand and the product, almost entirely absent from it.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between P/B and ROE?
options: The higher the ROE, the higher the acceptable P/B
P/B and ROE always move in exactly opposite directions
P/B divided by ROE gives the company's P/E ratio
The two ratios are entirely independent of each other
quiz.explanation: Every dong of equity generating a 20% return is worth far more than a dong generating 5%. This is why a high-ROE bank trades above 2x book while a low-ROE bank sits below 1x - and a P/B below 1 is usually an ROE problem, not a pricing problem.

keyTakeaways: P/B = Share price / Book Value per Share
Most useful for banks, insurance, real estate - where book value reflects real value closely
A low P/B doesn't automatically mean 'cheap' - asset quality and ROE need analyzing too

practicePrompt.question: A bank has a share price of 30,000 dong, with Book Value per Share (book value per share) = 25,000 dong. What is this bank's P/B, and why is P/B usually preferred for valuing banks over other industries?
options: P/B = 30,000/25,000 = 1.2x, a ratio that fits banks and insurers well
P/B = 25,000/30,000 = 0.83x, calculated by inverting book value over share price
P/B has no special meaning at all for the banking sector compared to other industries
P/B must always be greater than 2 for a bank to be considered fairly valued
practicePrompt.explanation: P/B = Share price / Book Value per Share = 30,000/25,000 = 1.2x. P/B is especially well-suited to banks, insurance, and real estate - industries whose balance sheet assets closely reflect real market value, unlike tech companies where value mostly comes from unrecorded intangible assets.

summary.keyIdea: P/B = Share price / Book Value per Share
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Most useful for banks, insurance, real estate - where book value reflects real value closely

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: If you're interested in a bank or real estate stock, look up its P/B and ask yourself: does the book value of this company reflect real value closely, or is there a lot of unrecorded intangible value?
application.secondary: P/B is only truly meaningful once you understand which industries it's suited for.

sections.text: When profit isn't the most reliable measure - as with a bank, where the assets on the books are almost exactly the real economic value - analysts turn to a different ratio: P/B.
The formula and which industries fit

P/B = Share price / Book Value per Share. This ratio is most useful for industries whose balance sheet assets reflect real economic value fairly accurately: banks (cash, loans), insurance, real estate. Bank analysts usually prioritize P/B over P/E because a bank's assets are recorded fairly closely to their real economic value on the books.

A P/B below 1 isn't necessarily a signal that a stock is a cheap buy - it can reflect genuine market concern about real asset quality (hidden bad debt at a bank, obsolete assets), or a company with a low ROE that doesn't deserve a valuation above book value. Conversely, a tech company with P/B = 15x isn't necessarily being unreasonably overvalued - its value lies mainly in INTANGIBLE assets (brand, algorithms, user data) not fully recorded on the balance sheet, which keeps Book Value (the denominator) 'naturally' small compared to real economic value.

items: A low P/B can be a genuine value opportunity - or a 'value trap' if asset quality is poor
Always combine P/B with ROE: a persistently low ROE reasonably comes with a low P/B
P/B is less meaningful for a company heavy in intangible assets (tech, consumer brands)
Banks, insurance, and real estate are the industries where P/B works best

lines: P/B is only trustworthy when the number on the books is close to economic reality - knowing when a ratio 'lies' matters just as much as knowing how to calculate it.
